strengths: Identifies a genuine and underappreciated gap in existing unlearning evaluation: misclassification of forget data (as used by UA) does not imply the true label has been excluded from the model's set of plausible predictions, and MIA's binary decision similarly ignores residual confidence in membership.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning two datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), two architectures (ResNet-18, ViT), random and class-wise forgetting scenarios, 9 unlearning methods, and multiple alpha/lambda settings, with results reported across many appendix tables with standard deviations from repeated trials.

The proposed CR and MIACR metrics, together with the mis-label/in-set analysis, provide additional diagnostic granularity beyond simple accuracy-based scores, and the Grad-CAM visualization (Table 1) offers an intuitive illustration of the phenomenon being targeted.

The proposed unlearning framework is designed as a general plug-in loss term (Eq. 9) compatible with existing training-based unlearning methods rather than a fully new pipeline, which aids adoptability.

Includes practical guidance and empirical exploration of calibration set size and alpha selection, plus an ablation (shadow/semi-shadow models) addressing distribution shift issues introduced by methods like Random Label.
weaknesses: The central methodological device—applying split conformal prediction to unlearned models—relies on exchangeability between calibration and evaluation data, which the paper explicitly acknowledges (footnote 1) may not hold in the unlearning setting, yet proceeds without any correction or theoretical justification beyond a caveat. This undermines the very statistical guarantee that motivates using conformal prediction over ad hoc alternatives, making the 'principled' framing somewhat oversold.

The CR metric (coverage/set-size ratio computed separately for Df and Dtest) is defined ad hoc; it is not clearly derived from any decision-theoretic or statistical principle, its values can exceed 1 (e.g., NegGrad+ in Table 5, CR=1.225), and its interpretation under the 'gap-to-RT' vs 'limit-based' criteria is not always consistent, making it hard to assess what a given CR value substantively implies about privacy/forgetting.

Evidence supporting the core motivating claim is mixed: Table 3/Table 8 show some methods (e.g., GA, SSD) have very low in-set ratios (6-8%) for misclassified points, meaning the described failure mode (true label surviving in the prediction set despite misclassification) is not universal across methods; the paper does not reconcile this heterogeneity with its general narrative that existing metrics are broadly insufficient.

The proposed unlearning framework's gains are modest and come with trade-offs (e.g., RA/TA degrade slightly as lambda increases; RL on ViT shows RA dropping to 94-95% with high variance), and there is no principled procedure for selecting lambda or alpha—results are reported for a small discrete grid without sensitivity analysis or guidance for practitioners.

The metrics and framework's dependence on alpha is substantial (coverage, set size, and CR all change considerably with alpha, and the paper notes 'overly high alpha values may skew evaluation results'), yet the recommended default (alpha=0.1) is asserted rather than justified via a rigorous coverage-validity analysis, weakening reproducibility of comparative conclusions across studies that might choose different alpha.

No comparison against alternative uncertainty-quantification-based unlearning evaluation baselines (e.g., the epistemic-uncertainty approach of Becker & Liebig, cited in related work but not empirically benchmarked), limiting the ability to judge whether CP-based metrics are uniquely useful versus other uncertainty measures.

The Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate and does not meaningfully discuss potential risks or limitations of using unvalidated conformal guarantees for privacy-sensitive claims (e.g., overstating that a method 'forgot' data when statistical validity may not hold).

Class-wise forgetting results (Appendix) show large calibration-size and qhat instability for some methods (e.g., Teacher with widely varying qhat_test 0.955→0.916), suggesting the calibration procedure's reliability under distribution shift is not fully solved even by the shadow-model heuristic proposed.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and reasonable limitation of standard unlearning metrics (UA, MIA): misclassification of forget data does not imply the true label has been fully excluded from the model's plausible prediction set, and the Grad-CAM illustration in Table 1 provides an intuitive qualitative motivation for this claim.

The empirical audit in Section 2.2 (Tables 2-3), showing that a substantial fraction of 'successfully forgotten' (misclassified) points still fall inside the conformal prediction set, is a useful diagnostic that supports the paper's motivating claim across several classic unlearning baselines.

Broad empirical coverage: experiments span two datasets/architectures (CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, Tiny ImageNet/ViT), random and class-wise forgetting, 9 unlearning methods, and multiple miscoverage levels, with an extensive appendix.
The proposed framework is presented as a plug-in loss term that can be added to the objective of any training-based unlearning method, which is a reasonable design choice for generality.
weaknesses: Circular validation: the proposed unlearning loss (Eq. 8) directly penalizes the same non-conformity-score-vs-threshold quantity that the CR/MIACR metrics measure. Consequently, showing that this loss improves CR/MIACR is close to optimizing-for-the-metric-you-invented rather than independent evidence of improved real-world forgetting/privacy; no external validation (e.g., actual membership-inference attacker success, distributional distance to a retrained model, or a different, independently motivated privacy metric) is used to corroborate that CR/MIACR improvements reflect genuine unlearning rather than confidence suppression on the forget set.

The method could plausibly be 'gamed' by simply lowering softmax confidence on forget-set points without genuine removal of learned information (an adversarial-style perturbation of confidence, not concept-level forgetting); the paper does not rule out or discuss this failure mode, which is central to whether the proposed loss represents true unlearning versus superficial score manipulation.

The paper's own footnote 1 acknowledges that the exchangeability assumption underlying conformal prediction's coverage guarantees does not hold in the unlearning setting, undermining the statistical foundation of both the evaluation metrics and the calibration step used inside the proposed loss; the only mitigation offered (a 'shadow model' trick in Appendix B.4) is applied post hoc to a single method (RL) and not integrated into the main methodology or theoretically justified.

CR metric behavior is unstable and non-monotonic in α, including cases where Set Size < 1 with near-empty prediction sets at higher α (explicitly noted in the paper), and the recommended default (α=0.1) appears chosen empirically/heuristically rather than principled; this raises concerns about the robustness and interpretability of the headline metric.

Potentially conflating 'forgetting quality' with general model degradation: FisherForgetting (FF) achieves the best (lowest) CR on Df but destroys overall accuracy (Table 4), which the paper dismisses qualitatively rather than analytically — this suggests CR may simply reward general prediction degradation/uncertainty rather than selective forgetting, weakening the central claim that CR is a more faithful measure than UA/MIA.

Limited algorithmic novelty: the core contribution (Eq. 7-8) is essentially the standard C&W margin loss with pt(x) replaced by a non-conformity score and the target threshold set to a periodically recomputed calibration quantile; this is an incremental adaptation rather than a substantively new unlearning mechanism.

The framework is only demonstrated on three simple baselines (RT, FT, RL); it is not shown to help (or even applied to) the methods identified in Section 2.4 as performing worst under CR (GA, Teacher, SSD, Salun), leaving the generality claim only partially supported.

Presentation issues: dense, hard-to-parse tables, minor writing errors (e.g., 'In addiction' in the conclusion, an unused/undefined notation zt(x) in Eq. 7), and the Impact Statement is boilerplate despite the paper's direct relevance to GDPR/privacy compliance, where a substantive ethical discussion would be expected.

No theoretical or convergence analysis of the proposed loss is provided; the choice of hyperparameters (Δ=0.01, λ) is empirical and the trade-off with predictive performance at higher λ (Table 16, λ=1) shows non-trivial RA/TA degradation that is not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely interesting and underexplored gap in machine unlearning evaluation: standard metrics like UA and MIA only check whether the *argmax* prediction changes, ignoring whether the true label remains a plausible candidate under uncertainty quantification. The empirical demonstration in Table 3 (30-85% of 'forgotten' misclassified points still fall in the conformal prediction set) is a compelling and concrete illustration of this gap, reinforced nicely by the Grad-CAM visualization in Table 1.
The proposed CR and MIACR metrics are simple, interpretable, and easy to compute on top of any existing unlearning pipeline, making them a low-cost addition to the evaluation toolkit.

Experimental coverage is extensive: two datasets/architectures (CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, Tiny ImageNet/ViT), both random and class-wise forgetting, nine unlearning baselines, multiple alpha levels, multiple random trials with standard deviations, and substantial supplementary analysis (calibration-set-size stability, shadow-model correction for distribution shift).

The proposed unlearning framework (C&W-style margin loss on non-conformity scores) is general and can be layered on top of existing training-based unlearning methods with a single loss term, and the experiments show consistent improvements in CR_Df while largely preserving TA/RA and CR_Dtest.

The paper is transparent about certain limitations, e.g. explicitly noting that conformal exchangeability may not strictly hold in the unlearning setting (footnote 1), and investigating the RL distribution-shift issue with a dedicated shadow-model fix in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core theoretical justification for the new metrics is weak: conformal prediction's coverage guarantees rely on exchangeability between calibration and test data, which the authors themselves acknowledge does not hold for forget data (footnote 1). The paper does not rigorously establish what CR/MIACR actually measure once this assumption is violated; it just asserts the concept is 'directly borrowed.' The ad-hoc shadow-model fix in Appendix B.4 is a symptom of this deeper issue rather than a principled solution.

Results are highly sensitive to the choice of alpha, and the paper's own analysis shows that at alpha=0.2 the Set Size frequently drops below 1 (near-empty sets), which the authors admit 'skews' the CR metric — yet method rankings under CR are reported and interpreted across alpha values without a clear guidance on which conclusions are robust versus artifacts of a poorly chosen threshold. The chosen default (alpha=0.1) appears somewhat arbitrary rather than derived from a principled criterion.

The 'gap to RT' and 'limit-based' evaluation criteria used to rank methods are informal heuristics rather than well-justified decision rules, and different criteria sometimes yield different 'best' methods (e.g., NegGrad+ vs RL), leaving the reader without clear guidance on how to weigh CR against traditional metrics in practice.

The proposed unlearning loss (Eq. 7-9) is a fairly direct adaptation of the C&W margin loss to non-conformity scores; the technical novelty is incremental relative to prior adversarial-loss-based approaches, and the method still requires tuning multiple hyperparameters (alpha, Delta, lambda) whose interactions are not deeply analyzed (Delta is fixed at 0.01 without justification or ablation).

The framework is only applicable to training-based unlearning methods, and evaluation is restricted to image classification with two architectures; there is no discussion or experiment addressing other modalities or training-free unlearning methods, limiting the demonstrated generality of the claims.

Presentation is dense and at times hard to parse (e.g., overloaded '(•)' gap notation, very large tables with minimal explanatory text in the body), which could hinder reproducibility and comprehension without careful reading of the appendix.

No computational cost/runtime comparison is provided for the added conformal calibration and C&W-style loss steps, which is relevant since conformal calibration data and additional forward passes add overhead to already expensive retraining-based baselines.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely interesting and underexplored issue: models that appear to 'forget' data under UA/MIA can still retain the true label within a conformal prediction set, exposing a 'fake unlearning' phenomenon that existing binary/accuracy-based metrics miss.

Extensive empirical study across two datasets (CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, Tiny ImageNet/ViT), two forgetting scenarios (random and class-wise), and 9 unlearning baselines, with ablations over confidence level, calibration set size, and hyperparameter λ.

The proposed CPU framework is simple, general, and can be added as a plug-in loss term to existing training-based unlearning methods without architectural changes, and shows consistent gains in UA (avg 6.6%) while largely preserving retain/test accuracy.
Good supporting qualitative evidence (Grad-CAM visualizations, softmax/loss distribution comparisons in the appendix) that helps intuitively support the 'fake unlearning' claim.
Reasonably transparent limitations section and an attempt to address a real complication (distribution shift for RL/SalUn) with a shadow-model calibration fix.
weaknesses: Potential circularity: the CPU framework's loss (Eq. 9) is explicitly designed to push the non-conformity score past the same threshold used to compute the proposed CR/MIACR metrics, so strong improvements on these metrics are close to a tautology; the paper would benefit from independent validation (e.g., stronger/adaptive MIA attacks, downstream privacy leakage tests, or human/qualitative checks) that these gains reflect genuine forgetting rather than metric-specific optimization.

Interpretability of CR is questionable: it is a ratio of coverage to average set size, so a model that simply becomes more uncertain (inflating set size for all classes, not just excluding the true label) would lower CR without necessarily achieving better 'forgetting' in a meaningful sense; the paper does not analyze or rule out this degenerate case carefully.

Conformal prediction guarantees rely on exchangeability between calibration and forget/test data; this assumption is plausibly violated after unlearning (e.g., RL/SalUn induce label-corrupted distribution shifts, addressed only via an ad hoc 'shadow model' calibration in the appendix). The core theoretical justification for CR/MIACR as calibrated, guarantee-backed metrics is thus weakened in exactly the setting the paper studies.

Some instability in the proposed framework's results (e.g., CPU-RL on Tiny ImageNet shows very large standard deviations, up to 20+ points, at higher λ), suggesting the method's forgetting/utility trade-off is not fully reliable in more challenging model/dataset combinations.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines two existing techniques (split conformal prediction and the C&W adversarial loss) in a straightforward way, without new theoretical results tying conformal set exclusion to any formal unlearning guarantee.
Evaluation is confined to image classification with two architectures; no experiments on other modalities or larger-scale settings, limiting generality claims despite the paper's broad framing.

Presentation could be tightened: notation is dense, several long tables in the main text are hard to parse, and there are minor formatting/duplication artifacts (e.g., near-duplicate content across the intro/related work), which reduce overall readability.

strengths: The paper investigates a genuinely interesting phenomenon: that unlearning methods judged effective by UA/MIA may still retain the true label within a conformal prediction set, an angle that has not been extensively explored in the unlearning literature.

The experimental protocol is broad, spanning CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, random and class-wise forgetting, 9 unlearning baselines, multiple confidence levels, and multiple random seeds with reported standard deviations.
Ablation studies on calibration set size and miscoverage rate provide some practical guidance for applying conformal prediction in this setting.
Grad-CAM visualizations offer an intuitive, qualitative complement to the quantitative claims about 'fake unlearning'.
weaknesses: The central premise is undermined by the paper's own data: the Retrain (RT) baseline, which by definition never sees the forget data and is treated throughout as the gold-standard oracle, itself exhibits substantial 'in-set' recovery ratios (30.6%-57.3% for UA, 32.0%-32.3% for MIA in Table 2/6). If even a model that never trained on the forget data shows this behavior, the 'fake unlearning' phenomenon largely reflects intrinsic conformal-set/model-uncertainty behavior on borderline examples rather than genuine retained information about the forget set, which the paper does not adequately address or control for (e.g., via comparison to conformal set sizes on ordinary unseen test data with matched accuracy).

The proposed CR metric (Coverage/Set Size) is an ad hoc ratio without theoretical justification connecting it to actual unlearning quality or privacy risk; unlike standard conformal prediction, no coverage guarantee or interpretability analysis is provided for this derived quantity, making its numeric values hard to interpret in isolation.

Two evaluation criteria (Gap-to-RT vs. Limit-based) are introduced and used somewhat interchangeably across the paper, at times producing different top-method rankings (e.g., Section 4.2), with no principled discussion of when one should trust one criterion over the other, weakening the reliability of the paper's comparative claims.

The proposed CPU framework's loss function is explicitly designed to push the non-conformity score of the true label beyond the same conformal threshold used to compute the CR metric, so improvements in CR under this framework are close to definitional/circular rather than independent evidence of improved 'true' forgetting; a more convincing validation would use an external, non-conformal-prediction-based signal (e.g., actual privacy attack success on held-out distributions or downstream membership inference under adaptive attacks).

The technical novelty of the unlearning loss (Eq. 9) is limited — it is a straightforward substitution of C&W margin-loss terms with conformal quantities, with no theoretical analysis of convergence, robustness, or why ∆=0.01 is an appropriate/robust margin choice.

No comparison against the one directly related work (Becker & Liebig, 2022) is provided empirically; it is only discussed qualitatively in related work, leaving open whether CR/MIACR offer real advantages over existing uncertainty-based unlearning evaluation approaches.

Coverage of experimental settings is restricted to image classification (acknowledged as a limitation), and no evidence is given that the conformal-prediction-based diagnosis or framework would generalize to more realistic unlearning use cases (e.g., LLMs, generative models) where much of current unlearning research interest lies.

Several presentation issues remain (e.g., 'In addiction' typo in the conclusion, duplicated/garbled early draft text in the introduction before the final contribution list, dense and hard-to-parse tables), suggesting the manuscript needs another editing pass.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and interesting gap in machine unlearning evaluation: existing metrics like UA and MIA are threshold-based (misclassification/binary decision) and can be 'fooled' when the true label remains a plausible candidate under uncertainty quantification. The empirical demonstration of this 'fake unlearning' phenomenon (Table 2/6, with 30-85% recovery ratios across methods) combined with Grad-CAM visualizations (Figure 1) is compelling and intuitive.

The proposed CR and MIACR metrics are simple, clearly defined, and directly motivated by the diagnosed problem. The paper provides two complementary evaluation criteria (gap-to-RT and limit-based) suited to different application contexts (privacy vs. bias removal), showing some methodological care.

The CPU unlearning framework is elegant: it reframes the C&W adversarial attack loss using the conformal non-conformity score and threshold, giving a principled way to push true labels out of the prediction set. It is presented as a lightweight, plug-in loss term (Eq. 10) applicable to any training-based unlearning method, which is a practically useful design choice.

The experimental scope is fairly extensive: 9 unlearning methods, 2 model/dataset combinations (CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, Tiny ImageNet/ViT), both random and class-wise forgetting scenarios, and thorough hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (calibration set size, α levels) with appendix results supporting the main claims.

The paper includes a reasonably honest limitations section and additional analyses (distribution shift handling for RL/Salun via shadow models, softmax/loss distribution comparisons in the appendix) that show attention to potential confounds.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for CR as Coverage/Set-Size is somewhat ad hoc; it is not derived from a decision-theoretic or information-theoretic principle, and no comparison against simpler alternatives (e.g., using Coverage or Set Size alone, or other combinations) is provided to justify this specific ratio.

The scope is restricted entirely to image classification (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), which is a comparatively narrow and somewhat dated setting for machine unlearning research; the paper does not discuss applicability to LLM unlearning or generative models, which are now central use cases for unlearning and where uncertainty quantification could be even more relevant. This substantially limits the practical significance of the contribution as currently demonstrated.

The framework's benefits are not consistently positive: for methods like RL that already over-forget, CPU further increases divergence (e.g., CPU-RL on Tiny ImageNet drives UA from 26.9% up to ~40% at λ=1, moving further from the RT target under criterion ➊), yet this over-forgetting trade-off is only briefly acknowledged rather than analyzed as a genuine limitation of the framework's generality.

Many reported improvements are small relative to the standard deviations shown in the tables (e.g., several CR/CRDtest gaps in Table 3/5 have deviations comparable to or larger than the reported differences), and no statistical significance testing is performed, making it hard to assess whether observed metric differences reflect real effects.

The claim that excluding the true label from the conformal set constitutes 'real forgetting' is asserted via correlational evidence (Grad-CAM, softmax/loss distributions) but not validated against an independent ground-truth notion of information leakage (e.g., stronger membership inference attacks, linear probing of intermediate representations, or extraction attacks), leaving open whether CR/MIACR truly capture deeper forgetting versus merely a stricter confidence threshold.

The related work section is thin (essentially one paragraph plus a single closely related prior work), underselling connections to the broader conformal prediction and privacy/uncertainty-quantification literature and making it harder to judge the incremental novelty relative to prior work combining CP with model evaluation.

The manuscript shows signs of insufficient proofreading (e.g., duplicated/garbled introductory content spanning pages 1-2 from what appears to be leftover draft text, occasional table/text numeric mismatches), which detracts from the presentation quality expected at this venue.
